notes.meaning: Here begins a second, longer list of Judah's family. "Descendants" here means family line, not just sons. Only Perez was Judah's own son; the others were grandsons or later relatives. The list is given mainly to trace Shobal's line back to Judah.
Shobal's line continues through Reaiah and Jahath. Jahath's sons started the families of the Zorathites, the people of the town of Zorah. This adds detail to what was said about them in chapter 2.

These families came from Hur. Many of the names, like Gedor and Hushah, are also the names of towns, so "father" often means the founder or leader of a place. Hur was the firstborn of his mother, Ephrathah, and his family settled Bethlehem. The list even names a sister, Hazzelelponi.
Ashhur, the founder of the town of Tekoa, had two wives. Ashhur was a son of Hezron born after his father died. Naarah's four sons are named here, though little else is known about them.
Helah's sons are listed next. Koz, whose family is named in verse 8, seems to belong with them. Some older writers think Jabez, in the next verse, came from this family of Koz.

Suddenly the list pauses for one man, Jabez. His name sounds like the Hebrew word for "pain" or "sorrow," because his birth was very hard for his mother. Even so, he grew up to be more honored than his brothers. Old commentators think he was honored for his faith and prayer, and the son who cost his mother the most pain became her greatest joy.

Jabez prayed to the God of Israel, the God who keeps His promises to His people. He asked God to bless him, to widen his land, to stay close to him, and to guard him from harm. He asked to be free from pain, a play on his own name. God answered, and his life became the opposite of his sad name.
Next comes the family of Chelub, who became the people of Recah. This Chelub is not the famous Caleb. Nothing more is known about these men or the place where they lived.

Kenaz's family includes Othniel, Israel's first judge, the leader God raised up to rescue His people. Joab, from this family, founded a valley of craftsmen, likely near Jerusalem. Families with the same trade often lived together and passed their skill down from parent to child. Working with your hands is honorable work.

This is Caleb son of Jephunneh, the brave spy who trusted God when others were afraid. His sons are named here, though nothing more is known of them. A name seems to have dropped out of the text before Kenaz.
The sons of Jehallelel are listed. Neither he nor his sons are mentioned anywhere else in the Bible.

Mered, a son of Ezrah, had two wives. One was Bithiah, a daughter of Pharaoh, and the other was from Judah. So an Egyptian princess became part of Judah's family, probably while Israel was still in Egypt. Many of the names here are towns that their children founded or led.
Hodiah's wife was the sister of Naham. Her sons led families in the towns of Keilah and Eshtemoa. How they connect to the people named earlier is not told.
Two more short family lists are given, for Shimon and for Ishi. Nothing else is known about these men. Some names seem to be missing at the end.

The list turns to Shelah, Judah's third son. His family included skilled linen weavers, who made fine cloth for kings and priests. Some of his family once ruled in Moab, probably after King David conquered it. The note that these are "ancient records" reminds readers that those great days were long past.
